{{smaller block|Only two mineral ''thickenings'' are at present employed: namely, kaolin and pipe-clay.

3. That which has become thick.

{{smaller block|Many small miliary deposits existed all over the peritoneum, resembling the whitish-yellow ''thickenings'' often found on the capsule of the spleen.
{{right|''Lancet'', 1890, I. 403.}}}}

'''thicket''' (thik′et), ''n.'' [< ME. *''thicket'', < AS. ''thiccet'' (pl. ''thiccetu''), a thicket, < ''thicce'', thick: see ''thick''.] A number of shrubs, bushes, or trees set and growing close together; a thick coppice, grove, or the like.

{{smaller block|As when a lion in a ''thicket'' pent,
Spying the boar all bent to combat him,
Makes through the shrubs and thunders as he goes.
{{right|''Peele'', Polyhymnia, l. 124 (Works, ed. Bullen, II. 293).}}}}

'''thicketed''' (thik′et-ed), ''a.'' [< ''thicket'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Abounding in thickets; covered with thick bushes or trees.

{{smaller block|These fields sloped down to a tiny streamlet with densely ''thicketed'' banks.
{{right|''H. Hayes'', Sons and Daughters, xviii.}}}}

'''thickety''' (thik′et-i), ''a.'' [< ''thicket'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Abounding in thickets. [Rare.]

'''thick-eyed''' (thik′īd), ''a.'' Dim-eyed; weak-sighted.

{{smaller block|''Thick-eyed'' musing and cursed melancholy.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 3. 49.}}}}

'''thickhead''' (thik′hed), ''n.'' 1. A stupid fellow; a blockhead; a numskull.—2. In ''ornith.'': (''a'') A shrike-like bird of the subfamily ''Pachycephalinæ''. See cut under ''Pachycephala''. (''b'') A scansorial barbet of the subfamily ''Capitoninæ''. ''Coues''. See cut under ''Capito''.—'''White-throated'''

{{RunningHeader|thick|6288|thick-legged}}{{smaller block|When the horse was laus, he gynneth gon . . .
Forth with "We hee," ''thurgh thikke and thurgh thenne.'' {{right|{{sc|Chaucer}}, Reeve's Tale, l. 146.}}}} {{smaller block|''Through thick and thin'', through mountains and through playns,
Those two great champions did attonce pursew
The fearefull damzell. {{right|{{sc|Spenser}}, F. Q., III. iv. 46.}}}} {{smaller block|To lie daily, ''through thick and thin'', and with every variety of circumstance and detail which a genius fertile in fiction could suggest, such was the simple rule prescribed by his [Alexander Farnese's] sovereign [Philip II.]. {{right|{{sc|Motley}}, Hist. Netherlands, II. 311.}}}} '''To lay it on thick''', to exaggerate; be extravagant, especially in laudation or flattery. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|He had been giving the squire a full and particular account — à la Henslowe — of my proceedings since I came. Henslowe ''lays it on thick'' — paints with a will. {{right|''Mrs. Humphry Ward'', Robert Elsmere, xviii.}}}} '''II.''' ''n.'' 1. The thickest part of anything. {{smaller|(''a'') That part which is of longest measurement across or through; the bulkiest part.}} {{smaller block|The freke . . .
Braid out a big sword, bare to hym sone
With a dedly dynt, & derit hym full euyll
Throgh the ''thicke'' of the thegh. {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 9021.}}}} {{smaller block|An' blacksmith 'e strips me the ''thick'' ov 'is airm, an' 'e shaws it to me. {{right|{{sc|Tennyson}}, Northern Cobbler.}}}} {{smaller|(''b'') The densest or most crowded part; the place of greatest resort or abundance.}} {{smaller block|Achimetes . . . in the ''thick'' of the dust and smoke presently entered his men. {{right|{{sc|Knolles}}.}}}} {{smaller block|I am plain Elia — no Selden, nor Archbishop Usher — though at present in the ''thick'' of their books. {{right|{{sc|Lamb}}, Oxford in the Vacation.}}}} {{smaller block|He has lived in the ''thick'' of people all his life. {{right|''W. M. Baker'', New Timothy, p. 104.}}}} {{smaller|(''d''†) To make obscure or dark; hence, to hide; conceal.}} {{smaller block|Hauing past three days and three nightes, forsaking all high wayes, ''thicked'' my self in the great desert, and being utterly tired, . . . and no lesse in feare of them that should seek mee, I conueyed my selfe into a great caue. {{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 144.}}}} '''II.''' ''intrans.'' To become thick. {{smaller block|But see, the Welkin ''thicks'' apace,
And stouping Phebus steepes his face. {{right|{{sc|Spenser}}, Shep. Cal., March.}}}} '''thick-and-thin''' (thik′ạnd-thin′), ''a.'' 1. Ready to go through thick and thin; thorough; devoted: as, a ''thick-and-thin'' supporter; a ''thick-and-thin'' advocate of a measure.—2. Having one sheave thicker than the other. Thick-and-thin blocks were formerly used as quarter-blocks under a yard. '''thickback''' (thik′bak), ''n.'' A kind of sole-fish, ''Solea variegata''. [Local, Eng.] '''thickbill''' (thik′bil), ''n.'' The bullfinch, ''Pyrrhula vulgaris''. See cut under ''bullfinch''. [Prov. Eng.] '''thick-brained''' (thik′brānd), ''a.'' Stupid; thick-skulled; thick-headed. {{smaller block|The ''thick-brain'd'' audience lively to awake. {{right|{{sc|Drayton}}, Sacrifice to Apollo.}}}} '''thick-coming''' (thik′kum″ing), ''a.'' Coming or following in close succession; crowding. {{smaller block|She is troubled with ''thick-coming'' fancies,
That keep her from her rest. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, v. 3. 38.}}}} '''thicken1''' (thik′n), ''v.'' [= Icel. ''thykkna'' = Sw. ''tjockna'' = Dan. ''tykne'', become thick; as ''thick'' + ''-en''1.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To become thick or (''c'') The spot of greatest intensity or activity. {{smaller block|He dressed as if life were a battle, and he were appointed to the ''thick'' of the fight. {{right|''T. Winthrop'', Cecil Dreeme, iv.}}}} 2. The time when anything is thickest. {{smaller block|In the ''thick'' of question and reply
I fled the house. {{right|''Tennyson'', The Sisters.}}}} 3. A thicket; a coppice. [Obsolete or prov. Eng.] {{smaller block|They must in fine condemned be to dwell
In ''thickes'' vnseene, in mewes for minyons made.
{{right|''Gascoigne'', Philomene (Steele Glas, etc., ed. Arber, p. 118).}}}} {{smaller block|Eft through the ''thicke'' they heard one rudely rush,
With noyse whereof he from his loftie steed
Downe fell to ground, and crept into a bush.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. iii. 21.}}}} 4. A stupid person; a dullard; a blockhead; a numskull. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|I told you how it would be. What a ''thick'' I was to come! {{right|''T. Hughes'', Tom Brown at Rugby, i. 7.}}}} '''thick''' (thik), ''adv.'' [< ME. ''thicke'', ''thikke'', < AS. ''thicce'', thick; from the adj.] In a thick manner, in any sense. {{smaller block|Quo for thro may noȝt thole, the ''thikker'' he sufferes.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), iii. 6.}}}} {{smaller block|He bethought hym full ''thicke'' in his throo hert,
And in his wit was he war of a wyle sone.
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 147.}}}} {{smaller block|The Tree is so ''thikke'' charged that it semethe that it wolde breke. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 168.}}}} {{smaller block|Speaking ''thick'', which nature made his blemish,
Became the accents of the valiant.
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 3. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|Plied ''thick'' and close as when the fight begun,
Their huge unwieldy navy wastes away.
{{right|''Dryden'', Annus Mirabilis, cxxv.}}}} thicker. (''a'') To grow dense. {{smaller block|Through his young woods how pleased Sabinus stray'd,
Or sate delighted in the ''thickening'' shade,
With annual joy the reddening shoots to greet.
{{right|''Pope'', Moral Essays, iv. 90.}}}} {{smaller block|No swelling twig puts forth its ''thickening'' leaves.
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 105.}}}} (''b'') To become deeper or heavier; gain bulk. {{smaller block|The downy flakes, . . .
Softly alighting upon all below,
Assimilate all objects. Earth receives
Gladly the ''thickening'' mantle.
{{right|''Cowper'', Task, iv. 330.}}}} (''c'') Of a liquid, to approach more nearly a state of solidity; gain firmer consistency; also, to become turbid or cloudy. (''d'') To become dark or obscure; specifically, of the weather, etc., to become misty or foggy. {{smaller block|Thy lustre ''thickens'',
When he shines by. ''Shak.'', A. and C., ii. 3. 27.}} {{smaller block|The weather still ''thickening'', and preventing a nearer approach to the land. {{right|''Cook'', Third Voyage, vi. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Through the ''thickening'' winter twilight, wide apart the battle rolled. {{right|''Whittier'', Angels of Buena Vista.}}}} (''e'') To grow more intense, profound, animated, intricate, etc.; become complicated. {{smaller block|''Bayes.'' Ay, now the Plot ''thickens'' very much upon us.
''Pret.'' What Oracle this darkness can evince?
Sometimes a Fishers Son, sometimes a Prince.
{{right|''Buckingham'', The Rehearsal, iii. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|The combat ''thickens'' like the storm that flies.
{{right|''Dryden'', Æneid, ix. 908.}}}} {{smaller block|A clamour ''thicken'd'', mixt with inmost terms
Of art and science. {{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, ii.}}}} (''f'') To gain in number or frequency; hence, to crowd; throng. {{smaller block|The gath'ring murmur spreads, their trampling feet}} {{smaller block|''Thick'' beats his heart, the troubled motions rise (So, ere a storm, the waters heave and roll). {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxi. 648.}}}} {{smaller block|So ''thick'' they died the people cried, "The gods are moved against the land." {{right|''Tennyson'', The Victim.}}}} '''Thick and threefold''', in quick succession, or in great numbers. {{smaller block|They came ''thick and threefold'' for a time, till an experienced stager discovered the plot. {{right|''Sir R. L'Estrange.''}}}} '''thick''' (thik), ''v.'' [< ME. ''thicken'', ''thikken'', < AS. ''thiccian'', make thick, < ''thicce'', thick: see ''thick'', ''a.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' To make thick; thicken. (''a'') To make close, dense, or compact; specifically, to make compact by fulling. {{smaller block|You may not forget to send some Western karseis, to wit dozens, which be ''thicked'' well. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', I. 358.}}}} {{smaller block|That no cap should be ''thicked'' or fulled in any mill untill the same had been well scoured and closed upon the bank, and half-footed at least upon the foot-stock. {{right|''Fuller'', Worthies, Monmouthshire. (''Richardson.'')}}}} (''b'') To increase in depth or girth; swell the proportions of (a solid body); fatten. {{smaller block|He [Pliny] writes also that caterpillars are bred by a dew, incrassated and ''thicked'' by the heat of the sun. {{right|''Rev. T. Adams'', Works, I. 79.}}}} (''c'') To give firmer consistency to; inspissate. {{smaller block|With sheeps milke ''thicked'' & salted they dresse and tan their hides. {{right|''Hakluyt's Voyages'', I. 99.}}}} {{smaller block|The Night-Mare Life-in-Death was she, Who ''thicks'' man's blood with cold. {{right|''Coleridge'', Ancient Mariner, iii.}}}} {{smaller block|Beat the loose sands, and ''thicken'' to the fleet. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, ii. 184.}}}} {{smaller block|I have not time to write any longer to you; but you may well expect our correspondence will ''thicken''. {{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 245.}}}} {{smaller block|The differences . . . became . . . numerous and complicated as the arrivals ''thickened''. {{right|''Dickens'', Dombey and Son, xiv.}}}} (''g'') To become indistinct. {{smaller block|Under the influence of which [port], . . . though the heart glows more and more, there comes a time when the brow clouds, and the speech ''thickens'', and the tongue refuses to act. {{right|''W. Besant'', Fifty Years Ago, p. 121.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' To make thick or thicker. (''a'') To make dense, close, or compact; specifically, to full, as cloth. {{smaller block|About which a bright ''thickned'' bush of golden haire did play, Which Vulcan forg'd him for his plume. {{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xix. 368.}}}} {{smaller block|Youngest Autumn, in a bower Grape-''thicken'd'' from the light, and blinded With many a deep-hued bell-like flower. {{right|''Tennyson'', Eleänore.}}}} (''b'') To increase in depth, or distance between opposite surfaces; hence, figuratively, to make stouter or more substantial; strengthen. {{smaller block|This may help to ''thicken'' other proofs That do demonstrate thinly. {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 430.}}}} {{smaller block|Now god-like Hector . . . Squadrons on squadrons drives, and fills the fields With close-rang'd chariots, and with ''thicken'd'' shields. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, viii. 261.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') Of liquids, to increase the consistency of; inspissate: as, to ''thicken'' gravy with flour; also, to render turbid or cloudy.}} {{smaller block|Whilst others ''thicken'' all the slimy dews,
And into purest honey work the juice. {{right|''Addison'', tr. of Virgil's Georgics, iv.}}}} {{smaller block|Water stop'd gives Birth
To Grass and Plants, and ''thickens'' into Earth. {{right|''Prior'', Solomon, i.}}}} {{smaller|(''d'') To obscure with clouds or mist; befog.}} {{smaller block|Now the ''thicken'd'' sky
Like a dark ceiling stood; down rush'd the rain. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., xi. 742.}}}} {{smaller|(''e'') To make more numerous or frequent; redouble: as, to ''thicken'' blows.}} '''thicken'''2 (thik′en), ''n.'' A spelling of ''thick 'un'' (which see, under ''thick'', ''a.''). '''thickener''' (thik′nėr), ''n.'' [< ''thicken''1 + ''-er''1.] One who or that which thickens; specifically, in ''calico-printing'', a substance used to give to the mordant or the dye such consistency as will prevent it from spreading too much, or to add to the weight of the fabric in the process of dyeing. {{smaller|Various materials are used, as gum arabic, gum Senegal, gum tragacanth, jalap, pipe-clay, dextrine, potato- and rice-starch, sulphate of lead, sugar, and molasses, but wheat-starch and flour are the best.}} '''thickening''' (thik′ning), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''thicken'', ''v.''] 1. The act or process of making or becoming thick. {{smaller block|The patient, as years pass on, shows other evidences of the gouty diathesis, such as . . . gouty ''thickenings'' of the cartilages of the pinna. {{right|''Lancet'', 1890, II. 116.}}}} 2. A substance used in making thick; specifically, in ''dyeing'' and ''calico-printing'', same as ''thickener''. {{smaller block|Only two mineral ''thickenings'' are at present employed: namely, kaolin and pipe-clay. {{right|''W. Crookes'', Dyeing and Calico-printing, p. 17.}}}} 3. That which has become thick. {{smaller block|Many small miliary deposits existed all over the peritoneum, resembling the whitish-yellow ''thickenings'' often found on the capsule of the spleen. {{right|''Lancet'', 1890, I. 403.}}}} '''thicket''' (thik′et), ''n.'' [< ME. *''thicket'', < AS. ''thiccet'' (pl. ''thiccetu''), a thicket, < ''thicce'', thick: see ''thick''.] A number of shrubs, bushes, or trees set and growing close together; a thick coppice, grove, or the like. {{smaller block|As when a lion in a ''thicket'' pent, Spying the boar all bent to combat him, Makes through the shrubs and thunders as he goes. {{right|''Peele'', Polyhymnia, l. 124 (Works, ed. Bullen, II. 293).}}}} '''thicketed''' (thik′et-ed), ''a.'' [< ''thicket'' + ''-ed''2.] Abounding in thickets; covered with thick bushes or trees. {{smaller block|These fields sloped down to a tiny streamlet with densely ''thicketed'' banks. {{right|''H. Hayes'', Sons and Daughters, xviii.}}}} '''thickety''' (thik′et-i), ''a.'' [< ''thicket'' + ''-y''1.] Abounding in thickets. [Rare.] '''thick-eyed''' (thik′īd), ''a.'' Dim-eyed; weak-sighted. {{smaller block|''Thick-eyed'' musing and cursed melancholy. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 3. 49.}}}} '''thickhead''' (thik′hed), ''n.'' 1. A stupid fellow; a blockhead; a numskull.—2. In ''ornith.'': (''a'') A shrike-like bird of the subfamily ''Pachycephalinæ''. See cut under ''Pachycephala''. (''b'') A scansorial barbet of the subfamily ''Capitoninæ''. ''Coues''. See cut under ''Capito''.—'''White-throated''' '''thickhead.''' {{smaller|Same as ''thunder-bird'', 1.}} '''thick-headed''' (thik′hed″ed), ''a.'' 1. Having a thick or bushy head. {{smaller block|Bring it near some ''thick-headed'' tree. {{right|''Mortimer'', Husbandry. (''Latham.'')}}}} 2. Having a thick skull; dull; stupid; doltish.—3. In ''Crustacea'', pachycephalous; of or pertaining to the ''Pachycephala''.—{{smaller|'''Thick-headed mullet, shrike,''' etc. See the nouns.}} '''thickknee''' (thik′nē), ''n.'' A bird of the family ''Œdicnemidæ;'' a thick-kneed plover, or stone-plover. {{smaller|The common thickknee of European countries is ''Œdicnemus crepitans'', also called ''Norfolk plover'' and by other names. See ''stone-plover'', and cut under ''Œdicnemus.''}} '''thick-kneed''' (thik′nēd), ''a.'' Having thick knees—that is, having the tibiotarsal articulation swollen or thickened, as the young of many wading birds: specifically noting the birds of the family ''Œdicnemidæ''. See cut under ''Œdicnemus''.—{{smaller|'''Thick-kneed bustard,''' a thickknee: it is not a bustard.}} '''thickleaf''' (thik′lēf), ''n.'' A plant of the genus ''Crassula''. '''thick-leaved''' (thik′lēvd), ''a.'' Having thick leaves; also, thickly set with leaves. {{smaller block|The nightingale, among the ''thick-leav'd'' spring That sits alone in sorrow. {{right|''Fletcher'', Faithful Shepherdess, v. 3.}}}} '''thick-legged''' (thik′leg″ed or -legd), ''a.'' Having thick legs, as an insect.—{{smaller|'''Thick-legged lily-beetles,''' the ''Lagriidæ'', as distinguished from the ''Crioceridæ''.}}
